standard_text: Apply the inverse relationship between squaring and finding the square root of a perfect square whole number. Find square roots of perfect square whole numbers.

progression.narrative:
This standard sets two linked goals: FIND the square root of a perfect square whole number, and APPLY the inverse relationship between squaring and finding a square root. Both rest on one fact -- a perfect square is a whole number times itself (n x n), and its square root is that n. So the progression opens where recognition lives: identifying which numbers are perfect squares, because a student who can't tell 36 from 20 can't root either one. From there the core verb arrives -- finding the square root by recalling the factor that produced the number (16 x 16 = 256, so the square root of 256 is 16), first as a plain calculation and then as a select-the-value task that baits the classic 'square root means divide by two' error.

The second half turns the fact into an inverse relationship students can run in both directions. Given a value, they choose the square-root expression that produces it (the square root of 169 gives 13, while 13 squared goes the other way to 169). Given a square-root equation, they undo the root by squaring to recover the number (the square root of x = 13 means x = 169). The capstone reasons about the relationship itself: squaring and square-rooting cancel, so applying both returns the starting number, and students justify why. The through-line we keep naming: a square root asks 'what times itself?', squaring asks the reverse, and the two undo each other. The calculator is not allowed, so every value stays a perfect square at most 400 and every root is exact.

steps.rationale: The Below-proficiency demand and the entry point: you must recognize a number as a whole number times itself before you can take its root.
The standard's core verb -- find square roots of perfect square whole numbers -- by recalling which factor was squared, using the harder range up to 400.
The same finding step in a select-the-value format, exposing and correcting the halving and off-by-one errors before the inverse work begins.
The At-proficiency inverse relationship in the value-to-expression direction: to produce k you take the square root of k times k, not k squared.
The inverse relationship in the other direction: undo a square root by squaring to recover the number under it.
The Above-proficiency synthesis (DOK 2): apply squaring and square-rooting as inverse operations that cancel, and justify why.

skills.name: Recall square facts by multiplying a whole number by itself

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply a whole number by itself to build the square facts up to 20 x 20.

skills.i_do_script: Squaring a number means multiplying it by itself. Watch: 12 squared is 12 x 12 = 144, and 15 squared is 15 x 15 = 225. I keep a short list in my head: 11 x 11 = 121, 12 x 12 = 144, 13 x 13 = 169, on up to 20 x 20 = 400. Knowing these facts cold is what lets me find a square root fast, because a square root just asks 'which number did I multiply by itself?'

canonical_error.pattern: Doubles the number instead of multiplying it by itself
canonical_error.example: Says 12 squared is 24 (12 + 12) instead of 144 (12 x 12)
canonical_error.why: The student reads the exponent 2 as 'times 2' or 'add itself once' rather than 'use the number as a factor twice.' Squaring is n x n, not n + n or n x 2.

skills.item_template: A whole number (1-20) to square. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: What is 12 squared?
What is 15 x 15?
What is 9 squared?
What is 20 squared?
What is 13 x 13?
What is 7 squared?

redirect_script.stop: Squared means times itself, not times 2.
redirect_script.prompt: Write the number twice with a multiplication sign: 12 squared is 12 x 12. Multiply those, don't add or double.
redirect_script.praise: You used the number as a factor twice -- that's squaring.

vocabulary.definition: Multiplying a number by itself; 5 squared means 5 x 5 = 25.
A whole number equal to some whole number times itself, like 49 = 7 x 7.

worked_example_script.text: Write '14 squared' and read it as 14 x 14.
What is 14 x 14? Break it up if you need to.
14 x 14 = 196. That makes 196 a perfect square, because 14 is the number squared.
If a student says 28, ask 'did you multiply 14 by itself, or just double it?'
Your turn: what is 16 squared?

skills.name: Read the square root symbol as the inverse of squaring

prerequisite_skill.description: Read the radical symbol and state that taking a square root undoes squaring.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What does the square root of 36 ask you to find?

skills.i_do_script: The square root symbol asks a question: 'what number, multiplied by itself, gives this?' Squaring and taking a square root are inverse operations -- they undo each other, like addition and subtraction. Watch: the square root of 36 asks 'what times itself is 36?' The answer is 6, because 6 x 6 = 36. And if I square that 6, I land right back on 36. Square root and squaring are two directions of the same fact.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads a square root as 'divide by two' instead of 'undo the squaring'
canonical_error.example: Says the square root of 36 is 18 (half of 36) instead of 6
canonical_error.why: The student confuses a square root with halving because both feel like 'making the number smaller.' A square root asks which factor was multiplied by itself, not what half the number is.

skills.item_template: A square-root expression or a squaring/rooting pair. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: What does the square root of 36 ask you to find?
sample_items.answer: The number that multiplied by itself gives 36 (which is 6)

sample_items.stem: Squaring undoes ___.
The square root of 49 is 7. What is 7 squared?
What times itself equals 81?
Is the square root of 100 equal to 50 or 10?
Taking the square root of a number undoes what operation?

redirect_script.stop: A square root asks 'what times itself?', not half.
redirect_script.prompt: Read the symbol as a question: what number multiplied by itself gives this? Test your answer by squaring it to get the number back.
redirect_script.praise: You read the root as undoing a square -- that's the inverse relationship.

vocabulary.definition: The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the value; the square root of 25 is 5.
Two operations that undo each other, like squaring and taking a square root.

next_steps.if_fail: Review exponents and the radical symbol (6.EE.1).

worked_example_script.text: Write the square root of 49 using the words 'square root of 49.'

7, because 7 x 7 = 49. Squaring that 7 takes you right back to 49 -- the two operations undo each other.
If a student says 24.5, ask 'did you halve 49, or find what times itself makes 49?'
Your turn: what is the square root of 64, and what is 8 squared?

skills.name: Identify which numbers are perfect squares
skills.i_do_script: A perfect square is a whole number that equals some whole number times itself. To test a number, I ask 'is there a whole number that squares to it?' Watch: is 36 a perfect square? Yes -- 6 x 6 = 36. Is 20 a perfect square? No -- 4 x 4 = 16 and 5 x 5 = 25, and 20 sits between them with no whole number in the middle. I check each number against my square facts: 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81 are all perfect squares; numbers like 20 and 75 are not.

canonical_error.pattern: Labels a number a perfect square when it is merely even or close to one
canonical_error.example: Calls 20 a perfect square because it is even and near 16 and 25, though no whole number squares to it
canonical_error.why: The student checks for 'looks squarish' or evenness instead of testing whether a whole number times itself produces it. A perfect square must be exactly n x n for some whole number n.

skills.item_template: A set of numbers; student selects all that are perfect squares. Multi-select.

sample_items.stem: Choose all the numbers that are perfect squares: 16, 20, 36, 49, 75
Is 64 a perfect square?
Is 50 a perfect square?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 50 sits between 49 and 64 with no whole-number root.

sample_items.stem: Choose all the perfect squares: 81, 90, 100, 110

redirect_script.stop: Is there a whole number that squares to it?
redirect_script.prompt: Test the number against your square facts. If no whole number times itself lands exactly on it, it is not a perfect square -- being even or nearby doesn't count.
redirect_script.praise: You found the exact whole number that squares to it -- that's a perfect square.

vocabulary.definition: A whole number equal to some whole number times itself, like 49 = 7 x 7.
A whole number with no whole-number square root, like 20 or 75.

worked_example_script.text: List the perfect squares up to 100: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.
Is 45 on the list? Is 64 on the list?
64 is 8 x 8, so it's a perfect square. 45 is not -- nothing whole squares to 45.
If a student calls 45 a perfect square because it's 'close to 49,' ask 'what whole number times itself equals exactly 45?'
Your turn: which of 30, 36, 40 is a perfect square?

practice_problems.answer: No -- 9^2 = 81 and 10^2 = 100, and nothing whole squares to 90.

skills.name: Find the square root of a perfect square whole number
skills.i_do_script: To find a square root, I ask 'what whole number, multiplied by itself, gives this number?' Watch the square root of 256. I run through my square facts: 15 x 15 = 225, too small; 16 x 16 = 256 -- that's it. So the square root of 256 is 16. I am NOT dividing by 2; I'm finding the factor that was multiplied by itself. For 144, it's 12, because 12 x 12 = 144.

canonical_error.pattern: Halves the number instead of finding the factor that was squared
canonical_error.example: Says the square root of 256 is 128 (256 / 2) instead of 16
canonical_error.why: The student treats a square root like 'divide by two' because both shrink the number. A square root asks which whole number times itself gives the value, not what half of it is.

skills.item_template: A perfect square (100-400). Student finds its square root. Numeric response.

redirect_script.stop: Are you halving, or finding what times itself?
redirect_script.prompt: Run through your square facts until one lands exactly on the number: 16 x 16 = 256. Take that factor, not half the number.
redirect_script.praise: You found the factor that squares to it -- that's the square root.

vocabulary.definition: The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the value; the square root of 25 is 5.
A whole number equal to some whole number times itself, like 49 = 7 x 7.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'the square root of 196.'
Which whole number times itself gets close to 196? Try 13, then 14.
13 x 13 = 169, 14 x 14 = 196 -- exactly. So the square root of 196 is 14.
If a student writes 98, ask 'did you halve 196, or find what times itself makes 196?'
Your turn: the square root of 289.

practice_problems.answer: A square root is not half. 18 x 18 = 324, so the square root of 324 is 18. Marcus divided by 2 instead of finding the factor that squares to 324.

skills.name: Evaluate a square root of a perfect square and select its value
skills.i_do_script: When a square root is given with answer choices, I still find the whole number that squares to the value -- I don't just grab a nearby number. Watch the square root of 64 with choices 6, 7, 8, 32. I test: 8 x 8 = 64, so the answer is 8. The choice 32 is half of 64 (a trap), and 7 is close but 7 x 7 = 49, not 64. I lock in my pick by squaring it to check.

canonical_error.pattern: Picks a value one off from the true root, or the halved value, without checking by squaring
canonical_error.example: For the square root of 64 chooses 7 (because it feels close) instead of 8, or 32 (half)
canonical_error.why: The student estimates or grabs the nearest-looking choice instead of recalling the exact square fact and verifying 8 x 8 = 64. The correct root is the one whose square lands exactly on the value.

skills.name: Identify which square-root expression equals a given value
skills.i_do_script: Sometimes I'm given a value and must pick the expression that produces it. To match a square root to a value k, I look for the square root of k times k, because the square root of (k x k) is k. Watch: which expression equals 13? The square root of 169, because 13 x 13 = 169 and the square root of 169 is 13. The trap is 13 squared, which equals 169, not 13. Squaring and square-rooting are opposite directions, so I pick the one that lands on 13.

canonical_error.pattern: Confuses squaring with square-rooting, choosing k squared instead of the square root of k squared
canonical_error.example: For a value of 13, picks 13^2 (= 169) or the square root of a non-perfect square instead of the square root of 169
canonical_error.why: The student treats squaring and rooting as the same direction. To PRODUCE the value 13 you take the square root of 169; squaring 13 goes the other way and gives 169.

redirect_script.praise: You picked the square root that produces the value -- that's using the inverse the right direction.

vocabulary.definition: Two operations that undo each other, like squaring and taking a square root.

activities.title: Square vs Square Root
activities.instructions:
1. Read Priya's claim that 13^2 has a value of 13.
2. Compute 13^2 -- does it equal 13?
3. Choose the expression that really equals 13 and explain the direction.
4. Write the difference between squaring and taking a square root.

content.error_step: Priya squared 13 instead of taking a square root.
content.why: 13^2 = 169; to get 13 you take the square root of 169.

activities.title: Equals the Value or Equals Its Square
materials: Card set of expressions labeled with their k
activities.instructions:
1. Each card shows an expression and its k.
2. Sort into 'Equals the value k' or 'Equals k squared.'
3. Compute each to justify its column.
4. Debrief: which form does 'has a value of k' always ask for?

strategy_links.why: Contrasting a correct square-root expression with the squared-term trap is exactly a worked-example-plus-error study.
Choosing k squared instead of the root is a precise direction error a find-and-fix corrects.
Think-pair-share on 'which expression produces 13, and why' surfaces the square-vs-root reasoning for debate.

questioning_prompts: To produce this value, do you square or take a square root?
What is the value times itself -- which square root uses it?
Does squaring the value give you the value, or something bigger?
Which choice is a non-perfect-square root you can rule out?
How can you check the expression equals the target value?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student chooses k squared instead of the square root of k squared.
misconception_redirects.say: To land on the value k, take the square root of k times k. The square root of 169 gives 13; 13 squared goes the other way to 169.
misconception_redirects.praise: You picked the square root that produces the value -- that's using the inverse the right direction.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks the square root of a non-perfect square near the target.
misconception_redirects.say: Only a perfect square has a whole-number root. The value k comes from the square root of k times k -- a perfect square, not the number next to it.
misconception_redirects.praise: You chose the perfect-square radical that lands exactly on the value.

quick_checks.prompt: Which equals 12: the square root of 144 or 12^2?
quick_checks.look_for: The square root of 144. Picking 12^2 (= 144) confuses the two directions.

quick_checks.prompt: Which equals 15: the square root of 225 or the square root of 224?
quick_checks.look_for: The square root of 225. 224 isn't a perfect square, so it has no whole-number root.

sentence_starters: To get the value ___, I take the square root of ___.
___ squared is ___, which is the opposite direction.

worked_solution.stem: Which expression has a value of 17: the square root of 289 or 17^2?

steps.math: to land on 17, take the square root of 17 x 17
steps.annotation: Producing the value uses the square root.
So 17 is the square root of 289.

faded_example.stem: Which expression has a value of 14: the square root of 196 or 14^2?

steps.math: to get the value 14, use a square root
steps.annotation: Pick the inverse that lands on 14.
So 14 is the square root of 196.
Explain why 14^2 is the wrong direction.

skills.name: Solve a square-root equation by squaring to recover the number
skills.i_do_script: When an equation says the square root of x equals a number, I undo the square root by squaring that number -- because squaring reverses a square root. Watch: the square root of x = 13. To get x by itself, I square the 13: 13 x 13 = 169, so x = 169. I check by taking the square root of 169, which is 13. Undoing a square root means squaring -- not halving or doubling.

canonical_error.pattern: Leaves the value alone or halves/doubles it instead of squaring to recover x
canonical_error.example: For the square root of x = 13 writes x = 13, or x = 6.5, instead of x = 169
canonical_error.why: The student doesn't apply the inverse operation. A square root is undone by squaring: if the square root of x is 13, then x = 13 x 13 = 169.

skills.item_template: An equation of the form 'the square root of x = k' (with k^2 <= 400). Student solves for x. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: An equation is given: the square root of x = 13. What is the value of x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: x = 13^2 = 169. Leaving x = 13 or halving to 6.5 are the errors.

sample_items.stem: The square root of x = 16. Find x.
If the square root of x = 18, what is x?
A square has an area of x square feet and a side length of 15 feet. What is x?

redirect_script.stop: How do you undo a square root?
redirect_script.prompt: Square the number on the other side: the square root of x = 13 means x = 13 x 13 = 169. Squaring reverses the root -- don't halve or leave it.
redirect_script.praise: You squared to undo the root -- that's the inverse relationship.

vocabulary.definition: Two operations that undo each other, like squaring and taking a square root.
The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the value; the square root of 25 is 5.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'the square root of x = 12.'
What operation undoes a square root? What is 12 squared?
Squaring undoes it: 12 x 12 = 144, so x = 144. Check: the square root of 144 is 12.
If a student writes x = 6 or x = 12, ask 'what did you square to get x?'
Your turn: the square root of x = 17.

practice_problems.stem: What is 10 squared?
To undo a square root, you ___.
practice_problems.answer: square (multiply by itself)

practice_problems.stem: The square root of x = 13. Find x.
The square root of x = 16. Find x.
Leo solved the square root of x = 18. Find and fix his mistake.
shown_work: Leo wrote: 'the square root of x = 18, so x = 9 (half of 18).'
practice_problems.answer: To undo a square root you square, not halve: x = 18 x 18 = 324. Check: the square root of 324 = 18.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: halving instead of squaring.

practice_problems.stem: A square garden has a side length of 14 feet. What is its area?
practice_problems.answer: 196 square feet (14^2).

practice_problems.stem: The square root of x = 20. What is x, and why is 20 the largest side length in range?
practice_problems.answer: x = 400; 20^2 = 400, the largest perfect square at most 400.

practice_problems.stem: Explain the steps to solve the square root of x = 15 without a calculator.
practice_problems.answer: Square both sides: 15 x 15 = 225, so x = 225. Squaring undoes the square root.

activities.title: Build the Square Back
activities.instructions:
1. Read an equation like the square root of x = 12.
2. Build a square that is 12 tiles on each side.
3. Count the total tiles -- that total is x.
4. Check that the square root of your total returns 12.
5. Debrief: why does counting the whole square give x, the number under the root?

activities.title: Square, Don't Halve
activities.instructions:
1. Read Leo's claim that the square root of x = 18 gives x = 9.
2. Ask: does the square root of 9 equal 18?
3. Square 18 to find the real x, then check.
4. Write the rule for undoing a square root.

content.worked_problem: The square root of x = 18. Leo wrote x = 9.
content.error_step: Leo halved 18 instead of squaring it.
content.why: To undo a square root, square: 18 x 18 = 324, so x = 324.

activities.title: Root Equation to Its x
activities.instructions:
1. Match each equation to the value of x that solves it.
2. Justify each match by squaring the root (the square root of x = 12 -> 144).
3. Check by taking the square root of x.
4. Debrief: which operation did every match use to find x?

strategy_links.why: Thinking aloud 'to undo a root I square it' models the inverse move students then internalize.
Halving instead of squaring is a precise error a find-and-fix with a check step corrects.
Gradual release from teacher-squared to student-squared builds independence on the inverse step.

questioning_prompts: What operation undoes a square root?
What is that number squared?
Did you halve, double, or square to find x?
How can you check x by taking its square root?
Why does squaring reverse a square root?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student leaves the value alone or halves/doubles it instead of squaring to recover x.
misconception_redirects.say: Square the number on the other side: the square root of x = 13 means x = 13 x 13 = 169. Squaring reverses the root -- don't halve or leave it.
misconception_redirects.praise: You squared to undo the root -- that's the inverse relationship.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student takes another square root of k instead of squaring.
misconception_redirects.say: You already have the root; to get x you go the other way and SQUARE it. The square root of x = 13 means x = 13 x 13 = 169.
misconception_redirects.praise: You squared to travel back to x -- the inverse of the root.

quick_checks.prompt: The square root of x = 12. Find x.
quick_checks.look_for: 144. An answer of 6 diagnoses halving; 12 means they didn't square.

quick_checks.prompt: The square root of x = 20. Find x.
quick_checks.look_for: 400. Anything but 400 means the squaring step was skipped.

sentence_starters: To undo the square root, I square ___: ___ x ___ = ___.
So x = ___, and checking, the square root of ___ is ___.

worked_solution.stem: Solve: the square root of x = 19.

steps.annotation: The root of x is given.

faded_example.stem: Solve: the square root of x = 14.

skills.name: Apply and justify the inverse relationship between squaring and square roots
skills.i_do_script: Squaring and taking a square root undo each other, so applying one right after the other returns the original number. Watch: (the square root of 25) squared. The square root of 25 is 5, and 5 squared is 25 -- back to the start. It works the other way too: the square root of (9 squared) = the square root of 81 = 9. To justify it, I say squaring is the inverse of taking a square root, so they cancel.

canonical_error.pattern: Applies only one operation and doesn't recognize the two cancel
canonical_error.example: Says (the square root of 25) squared = 5 (stopping at the root) instead of 25, or the square root of (9 squared) = 81 (stopping at the square) instead of 9
canonical_error.why: The student performs one operation and forgets the second, or doesn't see that squaring and rooting undo each other. Because they are inverses, doing both in either order returns the starting number.

skills.item_template: An expression combining a square root and a square, or a justification prompt about the inverse relationship. Multiple choice / short justification.

sample_items.stem: What is the value of (the square root of 25) squared?
sample_items.distractor_logic: sqrt(25) = 5, then 5^2 = 25. Stopping at 5 is the error.

sample_items.stem: What is the value of the square root of (9 squared)?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 9^2 = 81, then sqrt(81) = 9. Stopping at 81 is the error.

sample_items.stem: Which equation shows that squaring and taking a square root are inverse operations?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Only the first returns the original number after both operations.

sample_items.stem: What operation can be applied to the square root of 81 to equal 81? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Squaring -- because squaring is the inverse of taking a square root. The square root of 81 is 9, and 9 squared is 81.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Squaring the root returns the original 81.

redirect_script.stop: Did you do BOTH operations, or stop halfway?
redirect_script.prompt: Squaring and taking a square root undo each other. Do both: the square root of 25 is 5, then square the 5 to get back 25. Don't stop at the first step.
redirect_script.praise: You saw the two operations cancel back to the start -- that's the inverse relationship.

vocabulary.definition: Two operations that undo each other, like squaring and taking a square root.
Multiplying a number by itself; 5 squared means 5 x 5 = 25.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 8.NS.3 (estimate square roots of non-perfect squares).

worked_example_script.text: Write '(the square root of 49) squared.'
What is the square root of 49? Now what is that answer squared?
The square root of 49 is 7, and 7 squared is 49 -- you land back on 49. The two operations cancel.
If a student answers 7, ask 'did you square the 7 as the problem asks?'
Your turn: the square root of (4 squared).

practice_problems.stem: The square root of 25 is 5. What is 5 squared?
Squaring and taking a square root are ___ operations.
practice_problems.answer: inverse (they undo each other)

practice_problems.stem: What is (the square root of 25) squared?
What is the square root of (9 squared)?
Amir simplified (the square root of 36) squared. Find and fix his mistake.
shown_work: Amir wrote: '(the square root of 36) squared = 6.'
practice_problems.answer: Amir stopped after the square root. The square root of 36 is 6, and 6 squared is 36, so the value is 36. Squaring undoes the root and returns the original number.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: applying only one operation.

practice_problems.stem: Which equation shows the inverse relationship: (the square root of 16) squared = 16, or the square root of 16 = 16?
practice_problems.answer: (the square root of 16) squared = 16.

practice_problems.stem: A square has an area of 64 square feet. The side length is doubled. What is the new area?
practice_problems.answer: 256 square feet: side = the square root of 64 = 8 ft, doubled = 16 ft, new area = 16^2 = 256.
practice_problems.notes: Apply root then square in a context.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why (the square root of n) squared returns n for any perfect square n.
practice_problems.answer: The square root finds the factor that was squared, and squaring it multiplies that factor by itself again -- undoing the root and returning n.

activities.title: Cancels Back or Stops Halfway
materials: Card set of combined square/root statements
activities.instructions:
1. Each card shows a combined square-and-root statement with a result.
2. Sort into 'Returns the original number' or 'Only did one step.'
3. For each 'only did one step' card, finish the second operation to fix it.
4. Debrief: why do both operations together return the starting number?

activities.title: Do Both Steps
activities.instructions:
1. Read Amir's claim that (the square root of 36) squared = 6.
2. Do the square root, then the squaring -- write both steps.
3. State the final value and where Amir stopped.
4. Write one sentence justifying why the operations cancel.

content.worked_problem: (the square root of 36) squared. Amir wrote 6.
content.error_step: Amir stopped after the square root and skipped the squaring.
content.why: The square root of 36 is 6, and 6 squared is 36, so the value is 36.

activities.title: Justify the Inverse
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a prompt card and solve it out loud, both steps.
2. Say the justification: 'squaring and square-rooting are inverse, so they cancel to the start.'
3. The group gives a thumbs up only if both steps and the justification are stated.
4. Debrief: what one sentence always explains why these expressions simplify to the starting number?

strategy_links.why: Think-pair-share on 'why do these operations cancel' builds the DOK-2 justification the standard's top band asks for.
Journaling the general rule ('applying both inverse operations returns the start') consolidates the reasoning.
Studying a correct both-steps example beside a stopped-halfway one targets the single-operation error.

questioning_prompts: Did you do both operations, or stop after one?
What does the square root give you, and what does squaring it give back?
Why do squaring and square-rooting cancel?
Which equation returns the original number after both steps?
Can you justify your answer using inverse operations?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student applies only one operation and doesn't recognize the two cancel.
misconception_redirects.say: Squaring and taking a square root undo each other. Do both: the square root of 25 is 5, then square the 5 to get back 25. Don't stop at the first step.
misconception_redirects.praise: You saw the two operations cancel back to the start -- that's the inverse relationship.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student works the outside operation before the inside one.
misconception_redirects.say: Work from the inside out, then let the inverse cancel: the square root of (9 squared) = the square root of 81 = 9. Both orders return the original number.
misconception_redirects.praise: You applied both operations in order and saw them cancel to the start.

quick_checks.look_for: 16. An answer of 4 means the student stopped at the root.
5. An answer of 25 means they stopped at the square.

sentence_starters: The square root of ___ is ___, and ___ squared is ___, so I land back on ___.
Squaring and taking a square root are inverse, so they cancel to ___.

worked_solution.stem: Find the value of the square root of (12 squared).

steps.annotation: Squaring then rooting returns the original 12.

faded_example.stem: Find the value of (the square root of 81) squared.

steps.annotation: State the value and why the operations cancel.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S2 (find the square root of a perfect square) -- the standard's core computational demand. If they pass, move up to the inverse-relationship skills: S4 (match a value to its square-root expression) and S6 (apply and justify the inverse). If they fail, split: S1 checks whether they can even identify perfect squares, and S3 checks the easier multiple-choice evaluation. S5 (solve the square root of x = k by squaring) branches off as the inverse-direction check.
